items.title: Through three games, Ty Jerome is averaging more than a point per minute on 56/43/89 shooting splits — which, obviously, is ridiculous.
items.body_excerpt:
Through three games, Ty Jerome is averaging more than a point per minute on 56/43/89 shooting splits — which, obviously, is ridiculous.

What's even more ridiculous, though ... is that it might not actually be that ridiculous? tinyurl.com/uaz69x8

images.alt:
On the other, though … when Jerome has been on the court, he has been good. Often really good. During his healthiest season — 2024-25, when he played 70 games and nearly 1,400 minutes in Cleveland — Jerome broke out as an instant-offense maestro whose scoring and playmaking off the bench helped fuel the Cavaliers to a remarkable 64-win season that few saw coming.

That breakout turn earned Jerome a third-place finish in Sixth Man of the Year voting, and a three-year, $28 million contract with the Grizzlies. After returning to the floor in late January following the calf strain, Jerome was one of the most productive players in the entire NBA on a per-minute basis, averaging 19.7 points, 5.7 assists and 2.8 rebounds in just 22.7 minutes per game, while shooting 52% on 2-pointers, 42% on 3-pointers and 88% from the foul line. He did it cleanly, too, posting a 3.2-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio, and while contributing to the chaos on the defensive end, snagging a steal on more than 2% of opponents' offensive possessions and coming away with a block on more than 1% of their trips.

The Grizzlies scored 8.3 more points per 100 possessions with Jerome on the floor than off it last season, according to Cleaning the Glass — the largest offensive on/off split on the team, and one of the largest of any player in the league. The combination of high-volume scoring, high-efficiency shooting despite a sky-high usage rate and consistent turnover avoidance made Jerome something of an analytics marvel in his late-season surge. Among players who logged at least 300 minutes, Jerome finished seventh in the NBA in estimated plus-minus and box plus-minus, eighth in player efficiency rating, and either in or just outside the top 25 in win shares per 48 minutes, ESPN's net points added per 100 possessions, and The BBall Index's LEBRON.

The Pistons had the best record (18-7) in games played between Eastern Conference playoff teams last season, and they’ve begun the new year with impressive wins over the Celtics, Heat and Sixers. They had a rest advantage for their wire-to-wire victory in Philadelphia on Sunday, but were without Jalen Duren (out at least two weeks) and Ausar Thompson (ankle sprain).

Two takeaways

The Pistons made 14 or more 3-pointers in only 20 (24%) of their 82 games last season, but they’ve made at least 14 in all three games this year. They’ve seen the league’s second biggest jump in 3-point rate (from 35% to 43% of their shots), and they’ve shot 42.0% (third best) from beyond the arc, with Duncan Robinson 15-for-28 (54%).

The defense hasn’t been quite as tenacious as it was last season. That’s resulted in the league’s biggest drop in opponent turnover rate, but also its biggest drop in opponent free throw rate. Duren committed just two fouls in his 38 minutes against the Celtics and Heat.

Coming up: The Pistons swept the Knicks last season (winning the three games by an average of 28 points), but didn’t get a chance of facing the champs in the playoffs. They’ll play (at least) four times this year, with the first meeting at Madison Square Garden on Tuesday.

www.axios.com/2026/10/26/t...

images.alt:
TM: There’s been a lot of controversy and press coverage of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion initiatives in Texas. How would you define DEI, and does it have any place in Texas universities?

CM: DEI has been something that we’ve all talked about, we’ve all probably experienced. For me, I don’t want there to be handcuffs on anybody who has access to higher education. Whether it’s the color of your skin or the financial implications, everybody should have an opportunity to go get higher education.

TM: A number of professors at public Texas universities have complained about being forced to change what they teach to comply with new guidelines against teaching “race and gender ideology.” Texas A&M, for example, recently forced a professor to cut a reading from Plato from his syllabus. What would you say to professors who are worried about censorship?

CM: I think I need some more time with board members to understand what the real issues are from that standpoint, so that we can make students feel comfortable, and we can make professors feel comfortable. I need to really familiarize myself with some of the issues that have gone on in the past and where we stand on those. But at the end of the day, we want to focus on student success. What are we teaching them that’s going to help them when they get into the workforce? When it comes to DEI, when it comes to, you know, professors and what we’re teaching, I will get myself up to speed on that.
